title: Competitive Intelligence for Sales Teams: What Reps Use
summary: Competitive intelligence for sales teams, built around the deal: who else the buyer is evaluating, what they care about, and how to get intel to reps in time.
body_markdown:
## What competitive intelligence for sales teams should answer


Competitive intelligence for sales teams is about the deal in front of the rep. Launch tracking and messaging analysis help product marketing. A rep needs answers about one account.


The questions come in order. First: which competitors this account might be evaluating, who at the account is running the evaluation, and what those people care about. Second: what the competitor charges, what they do better than you, and what they do worse.


If your CI program can’t answer the first three for a live deal, it’s market research.


## Why most sales CI goes unused


Most CI programs produce plenty of information that reps can’t use on a call.


Klue’s audits of battlecards found that only 43% include talk tracks and only 19% include proof points. Most cards explain the competitor and stop, so the rep finishes reading and still doesn’t know what to say.


In Crayon’s State of Competitive Intelligence report, 47% of CI professionals ranked quality of analysis as the most important factor, ahead of presentation and speed. Battlecard creation fell from 76% of teams to 58% over two years, as programs moved toward delivering insight inside the tools reps already use.


Reps need to know whether the competitor is in this deal and what to say about it. Sales leaders tell us that without that context, reps fall back on weak signals like an old funding announcement, and then don’t act on them, because nothing in the signal says the account is buying.


## The six pieces of intel that change a deal


Build a sales CI program around these six:


1. **Which competitors are in the account.** Already installed, being evaluated, or both.
2. **Who is evaluating.** The people at the account meeting with vendors, and their roles.
3. **What those people care about.** The priorities and problems you learn in discovery.
4. **The competitor’s pricing.** How they package and discount.
5. **Where the competitor is stronger.** Be honest about it. Buyers already know.
6. **Where you are stronger.** Tied to the priorities in item three, not a generic feature list.


When we ask sales leaders about their blind spots, they name the top of this list: which accounts already use a competitor, which open deals a competitor is in, and how they do against each competitor in win-loss.


The first three items change with every deal and belong to the rep and account team. The last three change with every competitor and belong to whoever runs the CI program. Putting both in one document is one reason battlecards go stale while deal notes stay empty.


## How to find out who else is in the deal


Ask “who else are you looking at?” on a first call and you’ll usually get a polite non-answer.


Instead, name the problem you heard and play it back. Then ask how they’re solving it today: building something in-house, doing nothing, or looking at vendors. It doesn’t name a competitor or ask for a list, so it’s easy to answer. Buyers who see you on their side of the table are far more likely to tell you who else is in the deal.


One sales leader we spoke with kept losing late-stage deals on competitor pricing. They wanted to know which competitor was in the deal during discovery, while there was still time to shape the evaluation.


Once you know, log the competitor on the opportunity. Without that field, win-loss analysis by competitor is guesswork.


## Using the intel: outcomes over feature grids


Once you know the competitor, skip the feature comparison. Sell the outcome the buyer described in discovery and show how you deliver it.


Back it with social proof about why teams like theirs pick you, tailored to this buyer and repeated until it sticks. If you don’t position yourself against the competitor, their AE will do it for you, and not favorably.


Give the competitor credit where it’s due. The Competitive Intelligence Alliance teaches a four-step framework for this: validate, acknowledge, reframe, specify. Ask what’s driving the comparison, credit their strengths, reframe around the problem they solve less well, then show proof.


I once talked with a former AE at a long-established enterprise software vendor, from the period when newer AI-native challengers entered his category. When a buyer was also looking at a challenger, he told them to hear the challenger out. His product fit large, risk-averse enterprises that wanted a track record. It didn’t fit everyone, and both sides knew it. Recommending a competitor when it fits earns trust, and sellers who stay on the customer’s side close the right deals faster.


## Deliver intel where reps already work


Deliver CI just in time, not just in case. Put the intel in the CRM record, the deal’s Slack channel or the call prep doc.


Keep the top of every battlecard short: a one-line description of the competitor and three to five bullets a rep can read in two minutes.


Make it two-way. Crayon found that when CI updates go out ad hoc or quarterly, reps rarely or never send intel back. Only 25% of CI professionals use call recordings to feed their programs, even though sales calls are where competitor names come up.


Split versions where needs differ. A BDR making cold calls needs two lines and a question to ask. An AE running a demo needs the comparison and the proof.


## The gap battlecards can’t close: deals you never hear about


Everything above assumes you know the deal exists. Across competitive deals we hear the same pattern. Teams win often once they’re in an evaluation, but keep losing deals they never knew about, or join late after a competitor has already shaped the requirements.


Battlecards, competitor monitoring and win-loss work once a competitor is named in a deal. They can’t show you which accounts are evaluating a competitor without you.
